summary: Analyzes the history of how transient numeric identifiers were specified and implemented in IETF protocols and how security and privacy suffered. It provides evidence that guidance is needed. It is a product of the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Numbers that identify things, like tickets, can be guessed if made badly. This tells the story of times that happened.

questions: why predictable identifiers are a security problem
why are predictable identifiers a security problem
how long did it take to fix TCP sequence number vulnerabilities
subtitle: How poor identifier design caused security failures for three decades

tldr.problem: For over 30 years, IETF protocols have used predictable transient numeric identifiers (like IP IDs, TCP sequence numbers, and port numbers), leading to widespread security and privacy vulnerabilities.
tldr.mechanism: This document traces the history of how weak identifier selection in protocols allowed attacks ranging from denial of service to data injection to user tracking.
tldr.outcome: The RFC demonstrates that specification and implementation failures around transient identifiers are recurring problems that require explicit guidance, which RFC 9415 and RFC 9416 now provide.

today: RFC 9414 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023. It analyzes the history and provides evidence supporting the guidance in RFC 9415 and the formal requirements in RFC 9416 (BCP 72). The document has not been obsoleted and remains the primary reference for understanding why transient identifier design matters.

sections.title: A Thirty-Year Pattern
sections.content:
Since the early 1980s, IETF protocols have employed transient numeric identifiers to distinguish protocol objects like datagrams, network interfaces, and transport connections. Examples include IPv4 and IPv6 Identification fields, TCP Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs), IPv6 Interface Identifiers, port numbers, and DNS query IDs.

For decades, implementations of these protocols have been vulnerable to predictable identifier selection, enabling attacks with effects ranging from denial of service to data injection to user tracking. The root cause: insufficient or misleading protocol specifications that either failed to specify identifier generation requirements or suggested flawed algorithms like simple counters.
sections.plainLanguage: Network packets need ID numbers to work correctly. Bad design allowed attackers to guess these numbers, causing serious problems. This happened over and over.

sections.title: What Are Transient Numeric Identifiers
sections.content:
A transient numeric identifier is any value in a protocol that distinguishes one protocol object from another for a limited time. These identifiers are usually required to be unique within a specific context (like per network interface or per connection endpoint) during a time window (like the maximum lifetime a packet can travel).

The term encompasses diverse identifiers with different requirements: some must be unique within seconds, others within months; some must be unpredictable, others merely non-repeating. This variety led designers to overlook that predictability—even when uniqueness was achieved—could enable security attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Identifiers are like ticket numbers or house addresses. Each needs to be different from others in its group, and they shouldn't be easy to guess.

sections.title: Categories of Failures
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main reasons why transient identifier security has failed repeatedly. First, some specifications under-specified their identifiers, leaving implementation choices to vendors who often chose weak algorithms. TCP port specification (RFC 793) and DNS ID specification (RFC 1035) are historical examples. Second, some specifications over-specified identifiers by suggesting flawed algorithms like global counters for IPv6 Identification. Third, implementations sometimes failed to follow even weak specifications.

These failures span across protocol layers: IPv4 and IPv6 at the network layer, TCP at the transport layer, and DNS at the application layer. The pattern shows that security oversights in one protocol version were sometimes repeated in successor protocols, suggesting that explicit guidance was needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol writers either said too little about how to make ID numbers (leaving it to programmers who guessed wrong), said too much (suggesting bad methods), or programmers ignored the advice. All three caused problems.

sections.title: The IPv4 Identification Case Study
sections.content:
RFC 791 (1981) specified that IPv4 Identification values must be unique per {Source Address, Destination Address, Protocol} for the packet's lifetime, but suggested a global counter as one option. Implementations took this suggestion, creating predictable ID sequences. In 1998, researchers discovered these predictable IDs could count the number of packets a target host was sending—and later, execute sophisticated attacks like idle scanning and firewall probing. OpenBSD implemented randomization in response, but the issue affected IPv4 implementations for years.

When IPv6 was designed in 1995-1998, the IPv6 Identification field faced similar challenges despite the known IPv4 vulnerabilities. RFC 2460 even more explicitly suggested counters. It took until 2016 (RFC 7739) to publish guidance on secure IPv6 ID generation, and even then as an Informational, not Standards Track, document. The IPv6 case demonstrates how security lessons from one protocol can fail to transfer to its successor.
sections.plainLanguage: The story of ID numbers in IPv4 and IPv6 shows the problem clearly: bad advice was given, attackers found it 17 years later, fixes were slow, and the same mistakes happened with IPv6.

sections.title: Similar Patterns Across Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC documents parallel histories for TCP ISNs, ephemeral ports, DNS IDs, and IPv6 Interface Identifiers. Each shows the same cycle: initial specification with weak guidance or flawed suggestions, discovery of vulnerabilities years or decades later, slow adoption of fixes. TCP ISNs, specified with a global counter in 1981, remained vulnerable for 27 years until RFC 6528 (2012) provided formal guidance. DNS IDs, unspecified in 1987, enabled cache poisoning attacks by 1993 but weren't formally mandated to be randomized until RFC 5452 (2009).

One positive trend: as awareness grew, some responses accelerated. Port randomization guidance (RFC 6056) was adopted more rapidly than earlier fixes. This suggests that explicit, Standards Track guidance on transient identifier generation can influence implementations. However, even recent protocols may repeat historical mistakes if designers lack awareness of these lessons.
sections.plainLanguage: Over three decades, the same kind of problem kept happening with different numbers in different protocols. Each time it took years to realize the problem and years more to fix it.

sections.title: Lesson and Guidance
sections.content:
RFC 9414 is an Informational document that motivates the need for explicit guidance. It shows that advice in this area is warranted because specifications and implementations repeatedly made the same mistakes. The RFC is a product of the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group (PEARG) and represents consensus that transient identifier generation deserves protocol designer attention.

The RFC points to RFC 9415 and RFC 9416 as the response: RFC 9415 categorizes transient identifiers by their interoperability requirements and failure severity, then recommends specific algorithms for each category. RFC 9416 makes this guidance formal requirements for new IETF specifications. RFC 9414 provides the historical evidence that such guidance is not merely academic but essential for protocol security and privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC tells the story to show why the internet needs rules about making ID numbers safely. The other two RFCs (9415 and 9416) are those rules.
